1-3: The resin smokes and burns. Nothing else happens, which is the point.
4-5: The lettered walls weep a little more, as if in answer.
6-7: The signifer appears in the doorway and stands to attention until the smoke is gone.
8-9: A shepherd watches from the slope, and will tell Kohlergrund the old rite is kept again.
10-11: The signifer salutes, and says a few words of Latin: the name of his century.
12+: The smoke goes straight down through the floor, and the warmth under it fades. (SG: The serpent settles deeper.)

neighbours.secrets:
The tower. A Roman signal tower of the Eighth Legion, raised in 74 when the legion built the Black Forest Road, beside Abnoba's grove (the Hochtannen). Its lowest storey stands: one room, with Abnoba's altar and the lettered walls, and under it the old strongroom, flooded. The upper storeys were timber and are long gone. The Founders took only the plain outer facing for the manor, never a lettered stone, which is why the inscriptions are whole.

Abnoba's grove. The Romans planted seven silver firs on the slope below as her grove, and the inscriptions here are to the lady of those trees: the Hochtannen. The eldest fir remembers the soldiers burning resin on this altar each winter.

Abnoba's due. The first drop of each winter's weeping, burned on the altar at the solstice with the watchword spoken ("Abnoba vigilat", the lady keeps watch), is her due; the rest is the covenant's 2 pawns. The rite is what the serpent answers to: gathering the resin keeps it hungry, and burning the due keeps it asleep. The Founders kept the rite from 1115 to 1210, which is why the signifer saluted them.

The pool. Since 1211 the resin has gone ungathered and dripped through the floor into the strongroom: 2 pawns a winter, 18 pawns of Intellego vis by Spring 1220, with the serpent coiled in it around the pay-chest.

The pay-chest. In a Roman fort the shrine of the standards had a strongroom under it for the pay-chest, and the signifer kept the century's savings: here the altar room is the shrine and the flooded cellar is the strongroom. The chest holds about four thousand silver denarii, the savings of eighty men, worth about forty Mythic Pounds to a moneyer (nearly half of what Wolfram owes Kalb), and the century's standard, its pole and silver discs. German custom, which the Sachsenspiegel is writing down about now, gives treasure buried deeper than a plough goes to the king: the silver is the Emperor's, and in the Ortenau the Emperor's officer is the Schultheiss at Offenburg.

Gaius Vettius's story. In 251 the serpent came up out of the springs for the resin, and his century kept it asleep by burning Abnoba's due each winter. In 260 the frontier fell and the legions withdrew behind the Rhine. The century was ordered out, but the pay-chest was in the strongroom with the serpent coiled around it: they could not take it, and the signifer could not leave it, because the men's savings were his to keep. He stayed at his post to wait for an officer to relieve him. No one came. That winter no one burned the due, and the serpent woke and killed him at the altar; then it drank and slept. He has kept the watch for nine and a half centuries since.

How to relieve him. The Holy Roman Emperor is Rome's heir, and Gaius would accept the Emperor's officer as an officer of Rome. Bring the Schultheiss of Offenburg up the ridge, hand him the chest, and let him dismiss the signifer from the watch: the ghost is relieved, the covenant wins imperial favour, and the Schultheiss is on its side against the baron. Or the covenant keeps the silver quietly, buys Wolfram's debt from Kalb with it, and leaves the ghost on watch.

neighbours.name: The Spinner's Hollow
neighbours.summary: A deep hollow an hour's walk east of the Stone House, where the firs lean together and grey webs hang between them like sails. The air is warm in winter. Travellers who stop to rest there hear someone humming, just out of sight.

levels.name: The Whispering Well
levels.see: Per + Awareness against 9 at the Hollow's floor: the webs there hang the wrong way, drawn downward as if something deep were breathing in
levels.enter: whisper a secret down the well
levels.notes:
Whisper into the well and the shaft answers in your own voice, a word behind, and then the stones of the well-head are gone and you are standing at the bottom of it, in a round hall of grey silk lit by nothing at all. The silk is warm and faintly sticky, and it carries sound: every strand you brush murmurs a scrap of something once whispered, a name, a sin, the place a purse was buried. Lanterns of moth-wing hang on threads and turn to watch you pass. Dame Haspel dances here with partners who never tire, and Jörg the Fiddler plays on a root that has grown up through the floor. Paths of silk run off in every direction, and all of them, sooner or later, slope down.
Hush stands where the paths begin. Its questions set the price of going on.

levels.name: The Wheel
levels.see: only from the Well: a warm light far down the silk, and the slow turning of a wheel
levels.enter: drink from the Spinner's cup, which also gives guest-right until the next dawn
levels.notes:
At the bottom of the silk the hall narrows to a chamber no larger than a cottage, and warmer than a hearth. A great wheel of pale wood turns in the middle of it, though no foot works the treadle, and its thread runs upward into a dark too high to see. The walls are skeins: thousands of them, grey as ash, stacked like a cloth merchant's bolts, and the air hums with them like a hive. There is a low table and a silver cup that is always full. There is a second stool by the wheel, worn smooth, as if someone sits there often. When voices rise, something vast shifts in the dark overhead, and the whole chamber creaks like a ship.
Time is slack here. A cup drunk and a song heard may be an hour outside, or a season: roll on Time at the Wheel when the characters leave, +3 if they ate anything but what the cup gave and +3 if they slept.

triggers.name: Haspel's word to the King
triggers.what: Whenever someone goes down to the Wheel: by the next new moon the King of the Black Mountain's hunt knows their face, from Dame Haspel. She knows who came and went, not what was whispered or agreed.

triggers.name: The Spinner's hoard
triggers.what: The Spinner's hoard grows by 2 pawns of Vim: update the hoard line in her Bestiary card's Vis (24 in 1220). A secret of the King's bargained at the Wheel that year adds 2 more; iron carried among the cocoons spoils 1 pawn for each scene it is there. At 40 pawns, her Might, she is ready. She opens her glamour to Hildegund's hands, and Hildegund becomes part of the story, a thread of the new Spinner (Living in the Story). At this rate that is the winter of 1228.

tables.name: What waits in the webs
tables.rows:
botch: The Spinner's own attention. She would like a word, and a secret.
1-2: Only the humming.
3-4: A lost traveller wrapped to the waist in silk, asleep and smiling.
5-6: Small grey folk at the edge of sight, who want a story for passage.
7-8: A skein of silk on a branch, offered for a price whispered into it.
9: A thread that hums with Hildegund's voice.
10+: The way opens deeper into the Hollow than it should go.

tables.name: Time at the Wheel
tables.rows:
botch: They leave by another way, and come out in some other faerie place of the Black Forest, where the King's people have noticed them.
1-3: No time at all. The light hasn't moved.
4-5: The hour they thought.
6-7: A day and a night.
8: A week. Dammërstein has sent someone to look for them.
9: A season, gone in an evening.
10-11: A year and a day.
12+: Seven years, as in the old songs.

tables.name: The thread pulls
tables.rows:
1: Only silence: the words simply aren't there.
2: A cough that turns into humming.
3: They say something else entirely, and believe it.
4: The words come out in Faerie Speech, which the listener can't follow.
5: A grey thread at the corner of the mouth, and the Spinner feels the tug.
6: They forget, for a day, that they ever knew it.
7: Their throat burns as if with iron: a Light Wound.
8: They dream of the Wheel that night, and wake with the urge to go back.
9: The Spinner hears that they tried.
10: Somewhere in the Hollow, Old Spindleshanks wakes and remembers their face.

tables.name: Iron below
tables.rows:
1-2: The webs draw back from the bearer, and the paths close ahead of them.
3-4: The courtiers won't dance, speak or eat while it is near.
5-6: Hush asks, "Would you bring a blade to a guest's table?", and the way down will not open.
7-8: The silk around the bearer chars and smokes. The Spinner knows at once.
9: Old Spindleshanks comes a little way down to see.
10: Guest-right is void for the bearer and everyone who came with them, until dawn.

tables.name: What the valley says of the Hollow
tables.rows:
1: Whisper her your secret and she'll let you pass. (SG: True, in its way.)
2: Never thank her. (SG: True: a thank-you is a bargain with the price left blank.)
3: Eat or drink at her wheel and you're safe until dawn. (SG: True: guest-right.)
4: Something big lives in the webs above the wheel, and it takes strays. (SG: True: Old Spindleshanks.)
5: The lady of the Hollow was a burner's wife once. (SG: False. She is the valley's own story.)
6: Carry iron in, and you won't come out. (SG: Half true: it voids guest-right.)
7: Jörg the fiddler went down sixty years ago to play for her, and he's playing still. (SG: True.)
8: A lady from the Stone House walked into the webs the autumn the magi left, and never came out. (SG: True: Hildegund, at the Wheel.)
9: Tell a secret aloud in the sun, to three people, and her web can't hold it. (SG: True: daylight cuts thread.)
10: Mother Agathe went down the Well once when she was young, with a message, and came back up. (SG: True: the forfeit's words, in 1180.)

diary.text: Hildegund of Merinita comes down into the Hollow and makes the Stone House's peace with the Spinner's people.
Jörg the Fiddler of Kohlergrund goes down into the webs to buy his wife Liese's secret, and does not come home.
Agathe of the valley, twenty years old, carries the covenant's price down for Hildegund: the real price of the pact. Her tongue has been still on it ever since.
No one comes down from the Stone House this year, or the next. The Spinner counts every season of it.
Hildegund of Merinita walks into the Hollow and does not come out.
New faces at the Stone House. Hush begins to ask about them.

neighbours.secrets:
Hildegund of Merinita sits on the second stool at the Wheel (level 2), spinning beside the Spinner, half guest and half thread. She is courteous, distracted and glad of company, and she thinks it is still the autumn of 1211. Spinning a thread with the silver spindle here brings her back to herself.

The roll tables: What she asks when a bargain is struck; Time at the Wheel on leaving the Wheel; The thread pulls when a bound teller fails the roll to speak a spun secret; Gossip at court at a feast or a dance; Iron below when someone carries iron beneath the Hollow's floor; What waits in the webs on the way in.

Hildegund is the pact's forfeit (see the Court's page): she stays at the Wheel until the arrears are paid.

neighbours.name: The Whispering Well
neighbours.summary: A dry Roman well at the bottom of the Hollow, its shaft hung with silk. Each autumn the spiders spin a silk there that holds the sound of whatever was whispered into the well that year. Hold a skein to your ear and you can hear it.

triggers.name: The silk is spun
triggers.what: 4 pawns of Vim silk, one skein to the pawn. Under the old pact each skein cost a whispered secret; without a renewed pact it is taken only at the Spinner's pleasure, if at all.

diary.text: The first skein of the silk pact: four pawns of Vim, each paid for with a whispered secret.
The great skein: the Founders swear the pact again under Binding Oath, with its forfeit, and pay for one great skein with a single great secret.
The last skeins paid for under the pact.
The silk is spun as ever, and left on the webs. Each skein unpaid goes on the Spinner's books.

tables.name: What the silk says
tables.rows:
1: Silence. Every skein on the near webs is mute.
2: A child counting in German, over and over, in a voice from long ago.
3: A Kohlergrund girl's wish: a husband, and his name.
4: A charcoal-burner cursing the baron's toll-men.
5: A tired woman's voice promising something "for the house".
6: A man in Latin, confessing what he never told any priest.
7: Adelheid von Schattenbach, counting what is owed to Kalb, and weeping.
8: Your own voice, saying something you haven't said yet.
9: Hush, at your shoulder: "Have you come to listen, or to pay?"
10: Five voices arguing in Latin, and one of them names a thing under the hill.

tables.name: What Kohlergrund whispers of the Well
tables.rows:
1: Whisper a wish into the well and the spiders keep it for a year. (SG: True: the silk holds it.)
2: The magi paid the spiders in secrets. (SG: True.)
3: No one has paid since the magi left, and the spiders are keeping count. (SG: True: the arrears.)
4: A skein of the silk will let you hear a dead man's last words. (SG: Half true: only if he whispered them into the well.)
5: The Roman who dug the well is still at the bottom. (SG: False.)
6: The lady of the Hollow will trade for anything but iron. (SG: True.)

tables.name: Drawing the silk
tables.rows:
botch: You take a skein that wasn't paid for. The webs go still all the way up to the light, and Hush is at your shoulder.
1-3: The skeins come away cleanly, each humming faintly with its year.
4-5: Small grey folk watching from the shaft's lip, counting.
6-7: One skein holds a voice you know, and it isn't your own.
8-9: Hush asks whose secret paid for this one.
10-11: A skein spun bright as daylight, from a secret someone gave freely. (SG: The Spinner values it highly.)
12+: The Spinner herself, at the top of the shaft, fond and amused, asking what the house means to pay.

neighbours.name: The Hochtannen
neighbours.summary: On the slope below the Stone House stands a grove of silver firs taller than any church in Strassburg. The oldest were saplings when the legionaries marched past. In the heat of midsummer the eldest weep a golden resin that smells of honey and lightning. The charcoal-burners won't cut them; they say the trees remember. The Baron of Schattenbach's men have marked the straightest with axe-blazes: beams for the cathedral works at Strassburg.

diary.text: The Eighth Legion builds the road through the forest, and plants seven silver firs below its tower as Abnoba's grove.
Hildegund of the Stone House gathers the eldest firs' resin for the first time, and learns their rule.
Agathe, twelve years old, follows Hildegund up to the grove and is taught to take the resin without angering the trees.
Ricardus Caespuus of Durenmar comes to see the trees at Matthaios's invitation, and takes a cutting from the eldest fir home to his glasshouse.
Agathe gathers the resin alone. No one comes down from the Stone House to take it.
After Gertrud, the baron gives Agathe his leave to gather, and begins selling her resin to the apothecaries of Strassburg.
Kalb's factor walks the grove with the baron's men, and they blaze the straightest firs as beams for Strassburg.

tables.name: Among the old firs
tables.rows:
1: Stillness, and the smell of honey and lightning.
2: Mother Agathe at the foot of the eldest fir with a clay pot, who tells you to keep your knife in its sheath.
3: A fresh axe-blaze, white on the bark of a fir.
4: Charcoal-burners going the long way round the grove.
5: Kalb's factor with a measuring rod and two of the baron's men, counting the eldest trees.
6: A fir that has wept nothing this year: someone has cut its bark.
7: Roman paving under the needles, running up toward the ridge.
8: A loggers' camp at the grove's edge, axes stacked, waiting for word from the baron.
9: In the hush under the eldest tree, the tramp of marching feet that aren't there.
10: One of the younger firs felled in the night. Its stump weeps, and the blazes on the eldest seven are fresh.

tables.name: What the charcoal-burners say
tables.rows:
1: The trees remember, and if you cut one, it will remember you. (SG: True, in its way.)
2: Mother Agathe talks to the trees, and they answer. (SG: Half true: she knows their rule.)
3: Midsummer resin cures any fever. (SG: Half true: it's vis, and Agathe's remedies use it.)
4: The baron sells the resin to the apothecaries in Strassburg. (SG: True.)
5: A Bonisagus took a cutting of the eldest tree away to grow under glass. (SG: True: at Durenmar.)
6: Giants planted the eldest seven before the Flood. (SG: False: the Romans did.)

tables.name: What the baron's men say
tables.rows:
1: Kalb wants the straightest seven for the cathedral roof. (SG: True.)
2: The baron owes Kalb more than his manors are worth. (SG: Close to true.)
3: The grove is the baron's by the old Duke's grant. (SG: False: his grant is timber and game, not the ground.)
4: The wizards on the spur are all dead, so nobody will object. (SG: False.)
5: A man who cut the bark of the eldest fir went blind. (SG: False, unless the storyguide wants it true.)
6: The felling starts this summer, whatever the old woman says. (SG: True: the Schattenbach Fellings.)

tables.name: The midsummer harvest
tables.rows:
botch: A knife slips and cuts the bark. The eldest fir stops weeping, and the grove is silent around you.
1-3: The resin comes, golden and smelling of honey and lightning.
4-5: Mother Agathe arrives with her pot and says you're doing it wrong, kindly.
6-7: The baron's men at the grove's edge, watching who takes what.
8-9: Under the eldest tree, the tramp of marching feet, and the smell of a Roman altar fire.
10-11: A sapling in the needles, grown from the eldest fir's seed.
12+: The eldest fir weeps more than it has in years, as if it were glad of you.

links.note: Who gathers the resin, and knows the rule
Whose glasshouse holds a cutting of the eldest fir

neighbours.secrets:
Abnoba's grove. When the Eighth Legion built the Black Forest Road, the Romans planted seven silver firs on this slope beside their tower, as a grove for Abnoba, the forest's lady, and honoured her in both places: the inscriptions on the ridge are to the lady of these trees. The trees remember being honoured, and that is the Magic aura. Silver firs live four or five centuries; the eldest seven are about eleven hundred years old, magical trees that would be dead three times over anywhere else. There is no spirit in them: the trees are the magic.

The resin. The eldest seven weep it at midsummer, a golden resin that smells of honey and lightning: 2 of the grove's 3 pawns of Herbam vis a year; the rest of the grove gives the third. Fell the eldest and the yield falls to 1.

Angering the trees. Take only what they weep, by hand, into a vessel that is not iron, at midsummer, and leave a little on the bark. Cut the bark or tap a tree, and it weeps nothing for seven years. Fell one, and its share is gone for good. Agathe learned the rule from Hildegund, and she is the only one living who knows it.

"The trees remember" is true. An Intellego Herbam reading of the eldest fir hears the Eighth Legion marching up the valley, and sees the soldiers burning resin on the altar in the tower each winter: a clue to the serpent under the Watchtower.

Whose resin it is. Wolfram's grant names timber and game, nothing more. Resin, like honey, mast and pasture, stays with whoever holds the ground, and the Founders' charter gives the Stone House the ground. A man may not use one right to destroy another's, so the Schultheiss at Offenburg would rule that Wolfram may fell the grove's ordinary firs but not the eldest seven, because felling them destroys the Stone House's resin. The resin Agathe has gathered with his leave was never his to give leave for, and the baron has been selling the covenant's vis to the apothecaries of Strassburg since 1216. When the covenant claims it, it takes that money from him: one more grudge, and one more lever.

Agathe's share. She gathers the resin as she always has, and will gather it for the Stone House if it asks her properly. She keeps one pawn in three for her remedies and her trouble, so the covenant has 2 pawns a year from her, or all 3 if it gathers itself, breaks the rule and offends her. A bargain with her, or one great favour, secures the resource for five years.

The cutting at Durenmar. In 1196 Ricardus Caespuus of Bonisagus came up the valley at Matthaios's invitation to see the trees, and wrote Of Fir and Resin. Its last chapter, ruined by damp, tells how he took a cutting from the eldest fir and grew it under glass. It lived. A Hochtannen sapling has grown in his glasshouse at Durenmar for twenty-four years, so if the grove falls, Abnoba's last tree is in a Bonisagus's glasshouse. A magus apprenticed at Durenmar may have walked past it a hundred times without knowing what it was.

The axes. The baron's men have blazed the straightest firs as beams for the cathedral works at Strassburg. Kalb wants the Hochtannen first, and the eldest seven are the ones he means.

neighbours.name: The Mirror Tarn
neighbours.summary:
A small round pool of black water in the valley below the manor, ringed with reeds that never move. Nothing ripples it, not wind or rain or a thrown stone, which sinks without a sound. The Kohlergrund women won't look into it. They say it shows you as you will be, not as you are, and that a girl who looked too long came home with a stranger's face.

Each spring, at the equinox, those who know how lay a sheet of clear glass on the water and lift it away with the reflection still held in it.

triggers.name: The equinox reflections
triggers.what: At the equinox the reflections can be lifted on clear glass laid on the water: 3 pawns of Imaginem, one to a pane, lifted with no face over the water. Four of Matthaios's panes are left in the Founders' tower; a pane can be used again once its vis is spent, but clear glass breaks, since the Unnatural Law doesn't protect it.

diary.text: Matthaios makes the first clear panes, and the Founders lift the tarn's reflections at the equinox for the first time.
A visitor from Dankmar lifts a pane at the equinox. No one at the Stone House remembers her afterwards.
Bärbel of Kohlergrund, sixteen, looks into the tarn from sunrise to sunset, and comes home with a stranger's face.
The last equinox the reflections are lifted.
No one lifts the reflections. Kyrillos still comes down to the water, alone.

tables.name: What the tarn shows
tables.rows:
botch: You can't look away. When you do, the sun has moved, and your reflection no longer looks surprised to see you.
1-3: Your reflection, startled to be seen, as always.
4-5: Your reflection a moment late, and annoyed about it.
6: A stone thrown from the far bank sinks without a sound or a ripple.
7: Kyrillos at the water's edge, looking at your reflection rather than at you.
8: A heron in the reeds that never moves. Its reflection looks calmly back at you.
9: For a moment your reflection is older, and it looks relieved.
10-11: A companion's reflection meets your eye calmly, unsurprised.
12+: A sliver of clear glass in the reeds, still holding someone's face.

tables.name: What the Kohlergrund women say
tables.rows:
1: It shows you as you'll be, not as you are. (SG: True.)
2: Bärbel looked too long and came home with a stranger's face. (SG: True.)
3: The magi used to lift faces off the water with glass. (SG: Half true: reflections, never faces.)
4: A lady came from far away to see it, and no one remembers her name. (SG: True: Orphedra.)
5: A stone thrown in makes no sound, because the tarn has no bottom. (SG: Half true: it's silent; no one knows how deep it is.)
6: The barefoot monk goes down there to see whether people are what they seem. (SG: True: Kyrillos.)

tables.name: Lifting the reflections
tables.rows:
botch: A face is caught in the pane as it comes up. Whose, you'll learn when it breaks.
1-3: The reflection lifts clean, the glass dark and heavy with it.
4-5: The reeds lean, for the first time, toward whoever holds the pane.
6-7: Kyrillos on the far bank, watching which face comes up.
8-9: A pane cracks in the lifting, and the reflection runs back into the water.
10-11: Bärbel from Kohlergrund, come to warn you not to lean so far out.
12+: The tarn gives up an old reflection: a woman's face, smooth as glass, from 1187. (SG: Orphedra's, left behind.)

links.note: Who uses it to see whether a thing is what it seems
Who lifted her own face in 1187

neighbours.secrets:
What it shows. Your reflection in the tarn is never quite right: it looks startled to be seen, or annoyed, as if you had caught it at something. What it hides when you look is the face you will have. Look long enough and it stops hiding, and shows you as you will be: that is where the valley's saying comes from.

Kyrillos's use. Only true things are caught out. A reflection that is not startled, that meets your eye calmly, belongs to something that is not what it seems: a glamour, an illusion, a faerie in borrowed shape, a spirit wearing a man. Kyrillos, who walks the Path of Seeming, has come down to the water for a century to see whether a thing is what it seems, and he still does. Matthaios cast no reflection here after 1200, and the tarn showed nothing at all where he stood.

The first rule: never look too long. Look from sunrise to sunset and the reflection stops being caught out and looks back at you as itself, and you take its face, the face you will have. It is Imaginem: it changes your appearance, not your years. Bärbel of Kohlergrund did, in 1198.

The second rule: never lift your own face. At the spring equinox a pane of clear glass laid on the water lifts the reflection away still held in it: 3 pawns of Imaginem a year, one to a pane, lifted with no face over the water. A pane holding your own face holds it: while the pane is whole your face does not change, and when it breaks every year it held back arrives at once. Orphedra of Dankmar did, in 1187.

The panes. Matthaios made them; he had the craft of glass and the spell for it (Breath of the Glassworker). Four are left, packed in wool in a crate in the Founders' tower: three for the harvest and one to spare. A pane can be used again once its vis is spent, but clear glass is not obsidian and the Unnatural Law does not hold it, so it breaks. New panes cost dear at Strassburg, or a magus can make them with Breath of the Glassworker (CrTe 15). Kyrillos knows how to lift the reflections, and Matthaios's notes in his sealed study say so too.

Nine springs lost. No one has lifted the reflections since 1211, and they are gone with the springs.

Orphedra's visit. In the spring of 1187 Orphedra of Merinita came from Dankmar to Hildegund, a sodalis of her House, to see the tarn. At the equinox she lifted a pane holding her own reflection and took it home, and before she left she clouded the household's memory of her with her illusions, which is why no one recalls the visit. Her unnaturally smooth skin is the pane's work. She left her study of the tarn, The Tarn and the Glass, with Hildegund as the price of her visit. The pane is at Dankmar: a lever on a dangerous neighbour, and a reason she might come back.

neighbours.name: Burg Schattenbach
neighbours.summary: A squat keep and palisade on a wet rock above the Schattenbach, half a day north of the Stone House, where the valley pinches to the narrows. A chain hangs across the river below it, and there are always a few men by the windlass.

diary.text: Duke Berthold IV gives the keep at the narrows to his ministerialis Eberhard von Schattenbach, with two manors and the forest of the Schattenbach.
Wolfram is born at the keep, Eberhard's grandson.
Wolfram's father dies, and Wolfram holds the keep. The debts begin the next year.
Wolfram's men ride up the valley to Kohlergrund for the first time, and take a forest penny from every hearth.
Adelheid's last child, Gertrud, comes too early. Mother Agathe keeps her alive.
The chain is hung across the narrows, the year the duke died.
A letter from Rudolf Kalb: he has bought every debt Wolfram owes in Strassburg.

tables.name: At the baron's hall
tables.rows:
1: A shut gate, and a bored serjant who won't send word up.
2: Utz the Black at the windlass, weighing your horses and your purse.
3: The toll for the chain has gone up since last season.
4: Adelheid at the accounts table, asking pointed questions about the Stone House's rents.
5: Little Gertrud, small and sickly, and a nurse who swears by Mother Agathe.
6: A Strassburg clerk in Kalb's employ, lodged in the best room.
7: Serjants grumbling that the forest penny came up short again.
8: Raftsmen held at the chain while the baron's men look over their timber.
9: A hired man who'll sell what he knows about the garrison.
10: Wolfram at table, hospitable and in debt, wanting a favour from the Stone House.

tables.name: Talk in the hall
tables.rows:
1: Kalb has bought every debt the baron owes in Strassburg. (SG: True.)
2: The garrison stays only as long as the pennies come. (SG: True.)
3: Nobody gave the baron the right to hang that chain; he hung it the year the duke died. (SG: True.)
4: The lady keeps the accounts and knows to the penny how close they are to ruin. (SG: True: Adelheid.)
5: Utz the Black has buried two lords, and he's choosing his third. (SG: Half true: he has served three and buried two.)
6: The baron means to have the spur once the wizards are gone. (SG: True, if he dares.)
7: Mother Agathe saved little Gertrud, so the lady won't hear a word against her. (SG: True.)
8: The Schultheiss at Offenburg is the only man the baron fears. (SG: Close to true.)
9: There's Roman silver up on the ridge, and the baron means to have it. (SG: False: he doesn't know of it yet.)
10: The Stone House's rents should come to the baron now the Zähringen are gone. (SG: False: the charter gives them to the Stone House, if the Emperor's officer confirms it.)

tables.name: Passing the chain
tables.rows:
1: The chain is down, the windlass unmanned, the toll-men at dinner.
2: A bridge-penny, and a look at whatever you're carrying.
3: Double the penny, because the baron's in a temper.
4: A raft held at the chain, its men arguing, and the toll-men glad of someone new to bother.
5: Utz the Black himself, who lets you pass and asks your names.
6: The chain up, the gate shut, and word that nobody passes until the baron says so.

neighbours.secrets: The garrison is ten hired serjants under Utz the Black, a Rottweil man who has served three lords and buried two: no knights, since a lord this poor keeps none. They are paid from the bridge-penny and the forest penny, and they stay only as long as the pennies come. Adelheid, Wolfram's wife, keeps the manors' accounts, and she knows to the penny how close they are to Kalb.

neighbours.name: Wolfram von Schattenbach
neighbours.summary:
A Swabian knight of forty with a scarred jaw, two poor manors, a damp keep, a dozen hard men and debts in Strassburg he can't pay. He is no great lord and knows it, and it has made him cruel. The carters call him the robber baron, and the valley has kept the baron. His men chain the Schattenbach at the narrows below his keep and take a bridge-penny from every raft and cart, though there is no bridge. Carters who argue lose a wheel; those who argue twice lose more.

He fells the old firs of the valley and rafts them down the Kinzig to the Rhine, and he calls the whole valley his forest, whatever the charters say.

tables.name: The baron's man at the gate
tables.rows:
1: A serjant who looks, counts the chimneys, and rides off without a word.
2: Utz the Black, asking politely who the new masters are, and how many men they keep.
3: A demand for the forest penny from the Stone House's own hearths.
4: A brace of hares and an invitation to dine at the keep. (SG: He wants to see them.)
5: Toll-men who've stopped Lutz's cart at the chain and want the covenant to pay for it.
6: A complaint that the covenant's folk took wood from "his" forest.
7: An offer to buy the spur's timber rights, for a sum he doesn't have. (SG: Kalb's money, if Kalb agrees.)
8: Adelheid's letter, not her husband's: little Gertrud is sick again, and is Mother Agathe up at the house?
9: Four riders at the gate in the evening, who won't say what they want and won't leave.
10: Wolfram himself, sober, asking what the Stone House would give to be left alone.

tables.name: What the carters say of the baron
tables.rows:
1: Argue at the chain once and you lose a wheel; argue twice and you lose more. (SG: True.)
2: He's sold his soul to a Strassburg moneylender. (SG: Half true: he's sold the forest's yield to Kalb, a cloth merchant.)
3: The duke's dead and nobody's told the baron whose man he is now. (SG: True.)
4: His lady keeps the books, and she's the clever one. (SG: True: Adelheid.)
5: He's soft on only one thing: the old woman who saved his girl. (SG: True: Agathe.)
6: There was never a bridge, so there's no right to a bridge-penny. (SG: True: the toll is unlawful.)

tables.name: The baron's mood
tables.rows:
1: Drunk, generous and dangerous: he offers you anything, and remembers none of it.
2: Sober and frightened, with Kalb's latest letter on the table.
3: Hunting, and furious to be interrupted.
4: Tender, at little Gertrud's bedside, and in no mood to talk business.
5: Cold and proud, insisting the whole valley is his forest.
6: Curious: he wants to see a wizard do something, and won't say why.

favours.what: Gertrud's life: Agathe kept his last child alive when she came too early
About ninety pounds, written as sales of the forest's yield and pledged on his forest rights, due at Martinmas 1222

neighbours.secrets:
His creditor in Strassburg has promised to clear every debt for the Hochtannen firs as beams for the cathedral works. He lets Mother Agathe take the resin because his wife's last child, little Gertrud, lived only by her hands, and because the apothecaries pay him for it; it is the one soft place in him.

He doesn't yet know the Stone House is lived in again. He has heard only that someone has lit the lamps, and he will send a man to look before the year is out.

His legitimate claim. Wolfram's grandfather Eberhard, a ministerialis of Duke Berthold IV, was given the keep at the narrows in about 1160, with two manors, the keeping of the narrows, and "the forest of the Schattenbach": its timber and its game, through the whole valley. The Founders held the land above the narrows; the Schattenbachs held the trees on it. Two grants from the same house overlap, and for fifty years nobody had to settle it: Eberhard and his son never cut above the narrows, and the Founders never asked them to. So Wolfram does have a right to the Hochtannen's timber, though not to the ground they stand on, the resin, or the rent of the people who live under them.

He has had no confirmed lord since February 1218, when Duke Berthold V died without a male heir and the Zähringen lands were divided. He hasn't noticed. He held from the duke, the duke is dead, and it has not occurred to him that his fiefs and his oath now wait on whoever has the duke's rights here, most likely the Emperor's Schultheiss at Offenburg. Nobody has come to tell him, and so nobody has stopped him: the chain went up that autumn.

The bridge-penny is unlawful: no lord ever granted a toll at the narrows, and there is no bridge. In April 1220 the Emperor promised the bishops that no new tolls would be raised in their lands without their consent; the Schattenbach timber goes down the Kinzig to Strassburg, so the Bishop of Strassburg and the boatmen's gild both have reasons to care, if someone brings it to them. The toll pays his men: cut it off and he can't keep them.

Magic is the wrong tool for him. A lord who dies by magic, or a knight charmed out of his rights, brings the Quaesitores and a charge of interfering with mundanes. The ways through are mundane: the charter, the Schultheiss, the bishop and the gild, Kalb's ledger, Mother Agathe, or his daughter.

The forest penny is partly lawful. The burners' clamps eat timber, and the timber is his, so he may rightly charge for the wood they cut. But he takes a penny from every hearth, herders' too, at a rate he set himself, without asking the Founders, who hold the ground. The duke let it pass in 1213; the Schultheiss at Offenburg would split it, a fair wood-fee from the burners and nothing from the herders. A wood-fee settled with the covenant is a way to secure Kohlergrund's rents without a fight (Kohlergrund's card).

Whose resin it is. Wolfram's grant names timber and game, nothing more. Resin, like honey, mast and pasture, stays with whoever holds the ground, and the Founders' charter gives the Stone House the ground. A man may not use one right to destroy another's, so the Schultheiss at Offenburg would rule that Wolfram may fell the grove's ordinary firs but not the eldest seven, because felling them destroys the Stone House's resin. The resin Agathe has gathered with his leave was never his to give leave for, and the baron has been selling the covenant's vis to the apothecaries of Strassburg since 1216. When the covenant claims it, it takes that money from him: one more grudge, and one more lever.

The legionaries' silver. Under the Abnoba Watchtower is a pay-chest of about four thousand denarii, some forty Mythic Pounds, nearly half Wolfram's debt to Kalb. It lies in a serpent's coils, and by custom it belongs to the Emperor (the Watchtower's card).

neighbours.name: The Schattenbach Fellings
neighbours.summary: The baron's axes are working up the valley, one season's felling at a time.

stages.title: The camp
stages.clues: Smoke at the valley mouth; sawpits; strangers on the road; the toll-men riding up to Kohlergrund for the forest penny.
stages.ignored: Kohlergrund's herders lose a sheep or two, and a burner's daughter stops walking to the spring alone.
stages.stopped: The loggers keep to the lower valley, for now.
stages.turned: The loggers bring news, and a little silver, to the Stone House.

stages.title: The marks
stages.clues: Kalb's factor in the valley again; fresh axe-blazes on the eldest firs.
stages.ignored: Kalb doubles his offer and the eldest Hochtannen, the ones that weep the resin, are marked for felling next spring. Agathe begs the baron to spare them; for the first time he laughs at her, and she comes to the Stone House instead. If the eldest fall, the resin gives 1 pawn, not 3.
stages.stopped: The eldest firs are spared, and Agathe owes the Stone House.
stages.turned: The covenant shows Wolfram the Founders' charter, or has it confirmed at Offenburg: the resin is the Stone House's, and his timber right can't be used to destroy it, so the eldest seven stand. Agathe brokers the rest. Wolfram fells his own lower slopes for Kalb instead, the resin is secured, and the baron owes the Stone House a grudging debt.

stages.title: The Hollow, and Martinmas
stages.clues: Loggers who lose their way, fall sick, wake far from camp; Kalb's factor talking of Martinmas.
stages.ignored: The axes turn east into the edge of the Spinner's Hollow. The Spinner answers, and Kohlergrund pays for it: children who sleep and won't wake, webs across the doors. At Martinmas Wolfram cannot pay, the forest rights pass to Kalb, and the valley's next master is a man who has never seen it and will sell every tree.
stages.stopped: The fellings turn away from the Hollow.
stages.turned: Before Martinmas the covenant buys Wolfram's debt from Kalb, or settles the toll and the forest rights at Offenburg: the forest stays with a lord who has to live beside the Stone House, and he owes it.

tables.name: How the fellings show this season
tables.rows:
1: Smoke from the loggers' camp at the valley mouth, and nothing more.
2: A sawpit dug beside the road, and strangers working it who don't speak the valley's German.
3: A raft of fir trunks jammed at the narrows, and the raftsmen cursing the chain.
4: The toll-men riding up to Kohlergrund for the forest penny, with more men than last time.
5: A herder's sheep found dead by the loggers' camp, and the loggers laughing about it.
6: Kalb's factor walking the slopes with a measuring rod, asking who owns the ruin.
7: Fresh axe-blazes, white on the bark, higher up the valley than before.
8: Mother Agathe on the road to the keep, to beg the baron for the old firs. (SG: From the second stage.)
9: Loggers lost overnight near the Hollow's edge, found asleep in silk. (SG: Only at the third stage.)
10: A felled fir across the Schattenbach, damming it, and Kohlergrund's herders gathering with sticks.

tables.name: In the loggers' camp
tables.rows:
1: Hard men, short of pay, who'll talk for a jug.
2: A foreman from the Kinzig who wants nothing to do with the old firs, and says so quietly.
3: A logger with a burned hand who swears the bark bit him.
4: Kalb's factor, sharing their fire and their bread, asking which trees are straightest.
5: A girl from Kohlergrund selling bread, and the men watching her too closely.
6: Silk across the path into the camp in the morning, and nobody will go out alone. (SG: Only once the axes near the Hollow.)

neighbours.secrets:
Agathe is never the target: she harvests with Wolfram's leave. The trouble is Kalb's money changing what the baron will allow. At the second stage she becomes an ally to win or lose.

Why now: Wolfram's lord died in 1218 and no one has confirmed his fiefs, so no one restrains him, and Kalb's pledge falls due at Martinmas 1222.

He contests two of the covenant's resources, and each has its Hook: the Hochtannen resin (the trees are his to fell by his grandfather's grant) and the Rents of the Kohlergrund (his forest penny). The Hollow is not his to contest; it is what happens if the axes go too far.
